intro: Choose the reversed cards you want to work with. Then we will find a familiar situation and explore it step by step.
cardsHelp: This is your saved nine-card spread. Select one or more reversed cards. Upright cards remain sources of support.
uprightHelp: There are no reversed cards in this spread. You can build on what already helps: choose a situation and continue to the Organon and Sphragis.
uprightExample: An example to explore: something important is progressing, and you want to keep doing what works.
exampleNote: These are examples to choose from. Select only what actually resembles your life.
spheresHelp: What would you like to change in this situation? Each direction includes an example; you can select more than one.
goalTitle: What would you like to do differently?
intakeHelp: On each screen, choose the option closest to your situation. The next options use your selected cards and answers.
questionTitle: What specific change are you hoping for?
domainTitle: Where is this happening in your life?
eventTitle: Which description best matches your situation now?
constraintTitle: What is getting in the way of your next step?
resourcesTitle: What can you already rely on?
unknownTitle: What do you still need to find out?
interviewHelp: Think of one recent incident. Every question includes an example. Your answer changes the next question; “I don’t know” and “Not applicable” also help choose the direction.
branchYes: Let’s build on what you have and check how you can use it.
branchNo: Let’s check another obstacle and find an option available to you.
branchSkipped: We will leave this question open and explore another part of the situation.
branchNotApplicable: We will set that topic aside and check another explanation.
holdingTitle: What may be slowing things down
movementTitle: What may change after your next step
forecastHelp: Let’s look at what may happen under your chosen conditions and how you would notice it. You can still practise if there is too little information for a forecast.
practiceHelp: The forecast is not determined yet. You can complete the practice, choose a manageable action and return with observations.
practiceReady: Your practice is ready. Record the result after you have tried it in real life.
notYet: I have not tried it yet. Save and return later.
yesExample: This happened in your chosen situation, and you remember a specific incident.
noExample: This has not happened in your chosen situation, or you have not managed it yet.
step_contact: If the agreement to talk still stands, ask one specific question. For example: “What are you willing to do, and by when?” Leave the other person free to decline.
step_independent: Start with something that needs no response from anyone else: a draft, a list of facts or your own option. Do not assume the other person has agreed.
step_small: Allow two minutes and stop after one item. If you have no time or energy, choose when to return to it.
step_ready: Use the available time for one complete step. Decide beforehand what will count as enough for today.
step_verify: Keep one observable result: a question sent, a finished draft, an explicit answer or a completed item. Later, compare your expectation with what happened.
step_pause: If even a small step is unavailable now, pause. Note the obstacle and when you can reassess your energy and circumstances.
step_fallback: If nothing changes after your step, check another explanation or make the task smaller. Repeating the same action does not guarantee a different result.
domain_creative: Creative work and your own project
domain_example_work: For example: a work assignment, payment, job search or a discussion about workload.
domain_example_study: For example: an exam, a difficult topic, learning a skill or feedback from a teacher.
domain_example_relationship: For example: silence after a conversation, different expectations of closeness or an agreement not kept.
domain_example_home: For example: household tasks, a family decision, shared expenses or personal space.
domain_example_creative: For example: unfinished work, reluctance to share a draft or too many ideas at once.
domain_example_time: For example: repeated postponements, too many commitments or difficulty restarting after a break.
domain_example_other: For example: a personal choice, waiting for an important answer or a task you keep putting off.
lens_example_agency: You are waiting for approval even though part of the decision is already yours to make.
lens_example_shadow: You interpret someone’s silence as rejection, but you do not yet know the reason.
lens_example_boundary: You take on too much and then feel angry or exhausted. You want to say what works for you.
lens_example_relationship: You seem to have an agreement, but each person understood the promise differently.
lens_example_integration: You know what you want but keep stopping before taking the first small step.
mechanism_resources: Time, energy or resources are short
mechanism_dependency: The next step depends on someone else
mechanism_boundary: More is expected than you can give
mechanism_pressure: There is urgency, pressure or conflict
mechanism_values: Two important wishes pull in different directions
mechanism_form: You have an idea but no clear plan
mechanism_rhythm: You start but struggle to keep going
situation_information: Something was promised or you are waiting for something, but there is no clear answer. You are left guessing what is happening.
situation_resources: The task matters, but one specific resource is missing: an hour, a sum of money, a skill or help.
situation_dependency: You have done your part and are waiting for someone else’s confirmation, decision or action.
situation_boundary: Requests keep coming and it is hard to say no. Your energy, money or personal time is being used beyond what you agreed to.
situation_pressure: You are expected to respond quickly amid an argument or a tight deadline. Pressure makes a calm, reversible step harder to choose.
situation_values: Both options offer something and each has a cost. For example: keep what is comfortable or take a risk for an important change.
situation_form: There are plenty of ideas and discussions, but it is unclear what should be finished first and what would count as good enough.
situation_rhythm: You have started before, but the task keeps being postponed. The step may be too large or may not fit into a normal day.
outcome_access: Get what is needed for the next step
outcome_accepted: Share an initial result and get feedback
outcome_example_response: For example: learn whether the answer is yes, no or conditional, instead of guessing from silence.
outcome_example_agreement: For example: agree who will do a task and when, with both people understanding the same promise.
outcome_example_access: For example: find time, gain access to materials or arrange help.
outcome_example_accepted: For example: share a draft, trial version or completed part and receive specific feedback.
outcome_example_milestone: For example: finish one application, one skill practice session or one step in a home project.
constraint_time: Constraint: there is only time for a short attempt.
constraint_information: Constraint: important information is still missing.
constraint_agreement: Constraint: another person’s involvement has not been agreed.
constraint_energy: Constraint: energy is low, so the effort needs to be reduced.
resource_note: Support: you can quietly write down your thoughts and facts.
resource_skill: Support: you already have the skill needed for a small part of the task.
resource_support: Support: someone has agreed to help.
resource_window: Support: time has been set aside without other commitments.
phase_first: This is the first such incident.
phase_repeated: A similar situation has happened before.
phase_changed: Things used to be different, but one condition has changed.
card_alpha: You want to begin but are waiting for permission or a perfect moment.
card_beta: You put in a lot but are unsure whether the effort is mutual.
card_gamma: You have an idea but struggle to turn it into an initial result.
card_delta: You hold on to a familiar arrangement even though it has become restrictive.
card_epsilon: You adapt to others’ expectations and lose sight of your own direction.
card_zeta: You want to force a breakthrough but do not have the energy for it.
card_eta: You spend more than you can replenish: money, attention or energy.
card_theta: You keep going out of habit when pausing to understand the situation might help.
card_iota: It is hard to tell your own wish apart from what you feel you ought to want.
card_kappa: The same task keeps starting over without steady follow-through.
card_lambda: You become the person everyone relies on, while support for you remains uncertain.
card_mu: Accumulated responsibilities consume the resources needed for something important.
card_nu: You notice conflicting signals and do not know which to trust.
card_xi: Another person is delaying while your plans depend on their decision.
card_omicron: An old habit brings you back to a situation you have already tried to change.
card_pi: It is hard to stop others’ demands and state a limit you can accept.
card_rho: Tension pushes you toward a sharp response you might later regret.
card_sigma: You try to speed up a process that first needs rest or a different pace.
card_tau: You are bound by a promise that now costs you something important.
card_upsilon: Two paths lie ahead, and each requires giving up something valuable.
card_phi: There are many words and explanations, but no clear agreement emerges.
card_chi: You put in effort, but the result does not match what you intended.
card_psi: Feelings are strong, making it difficult to decide what you actually want to do.
card_omega: The task is almost done, but the final step or closure keeps being postponed.
holding_information: Uncertainty leaves room for assumptions. Without a fact, several explanations remain possible.
holding_resources: The task may be larger than the available time, energy or resources.
holding_dependency: Your plan includes a step controlled by someone else.
holding_boundary: Expectations may differ: what feels like a request to one person may already overload the other.
holding_pressure: Urgency narrows the options and raises the cost of an impulsive decision.
holding_values: The decision is delayed because each option protects one value while affecting another.
holding_form: There is not yet a small result that can be produced and checked.
holding_rhythm: The action is hard to repeat at the pace and scale you have chosen.
movement_information: One verifiable answer can clarify what to expect and which option is no longer needed.
movement_resources: Making the step smaller can reveal whether you can progress with what you already have.
movement_dependency: A separate independent step lets you move while the other person’s decision remains open.
movement_boundary: Clearly stating what is acceptable helps you check whether others are willing to respect your limits.
movement_pressure: A pause and a reversible decision let you check the consequences without unnecessary urgency.
movement_values: A small, low-cost trial can help clarify which value matters most right now.
movement_form: A draft or trial gives you something concrete for the next decision.
movement_rhythm: A small repeatable step can reveal a pace you can actually maintain.
action_information: Write down one question whose answer would change your decision. For example: “Was the task accepted, or are revisions still needed?” Find a message or record that could verify it.
action_resources: Name one missing resource and the minimum amount needed. For example: “I need 15 quiet minutes to complete the first part of the application.”
action_dependency: Divide a page into “I can do this myself” and “I need someone else’s response”. Choose one item from the first part and prepare it.
action_boundary: Draft one short sentence about your limit. For example: “I can help for 20 minutes today; I can discuss the rest tomorrow.” First write it down for yourself.
action_pressure: Delay an irreversible response until a calmer moment. Write down what must be decided now and what can genuinely wait.
action_values: Write down two options and one important cost for each. Find a small trial that could teach you more without a final commitment.
action_form: Describe the result in one sentence: “At the end I will have…” Make the simplest draft: one paragraph, a sketch or the first item.
action_rhythm: Attach a two-minute step to an existing routine. For example: after breakfast, open the material and complete one item.
question_event_observed: Did you see what happened yourself?
example_event_observed: You read the message or saw the action, rather than only hearing someone’s explanation.
question_target_observable: Will you be able to tell when the desired change has happened?
example_target_observable: You can check a response, a finished item or a kept agreement; “things will get better” is harder to verify.
question_change_desired: Do you want to change something in this situation?
example_change_desired: You may want a new solution, or you may prefer to understand things and leave them as they are for now.
question_baseline_defined: Can you describe how things stand right now?
example_baseline_defined: For example: no reply for three days, one of five items completed, or an agreement still unconfirmed.
question_actor_role_known: Is it clear who is responsible for what here?
example_actor_role_known: For example: you prepare an option and another person approves it. A role that has not been discussed is not yet settled.
question_outcome_not_known: Is the result still ahead and unknown?
example_outcome_not_known: If the reply has arrived or the event has happened, you can reflect on it and choose what to do next.
question_event_order_known: Do you remember what happened first and what followed?
example_event_order_known: For example: the terms changed first, and the conversation became tense later. The sequence helps check a possible cause.
question_deadline_defined: Is there a specific agreed deadline?
example_deadline_defined: “By Friday” is a deadline. “When possible” or “soon” does not yet give a clear date.
question_lead_time_known: Do you know how long this kind of step usually takes?
example_lead_time_known: For example: replies used to arrive within two days. Without comparable cases, the duration is still unknown.
question_phase_known: Is it clear which stage you have reached?
example_phase_known: For example: preparation is complete but approval has not started, or a conversation happened without a decision.
question_condition_before_outcome: Do you know what must happen before the result is possible?
example_condition_before_outcome: For example: access is needed before work can start; both people must agree before a meeting.
question_horizon_defined: Have you chosen a day to check for changes?
example_horizon_defined: For example: return to your notes in a week and check whether a reply or an initial result has arrived.
question_repetition_known: Has something like this happened before?
example_repetition_known: Recall separate incidents: a promise, a wait and a similar outcome. One long wait still counts as one incident.
question_pattern_same_context: Were the circumstances broadly similar on previous occasions?
example_pattern_same_context: Compare the people, workload and agreements. If things are different this time, the previous pattern may not repeat.
question_prior_exception: Was there a time when things went differently and better?
example_prior_exception: For example: conversations usually broke down, but once you chose a calm time and reached an agreement.
question_attempted_again: Have you already tried the same approach again?
example_attempted_again: For example: you sent the same reminder again or restarted with the same ambitious plan.
question_earlier_result_observed: Do you know how the previous attempt ended?
example_earlier_result_observed: Separate “I sent a message” from “I received a reply”: one is your action and the other is the result.
question_earliest_difference: Did you notice what changed first in a successful attempt?
example_earliest_difference: For example: the task became smaller, the request more specific or the conversation less rushed.
question_direct_evidence: Do you have concrete evidence of what is happening?
example_direct_evidence: A message, document or action you observed can count. An assumption about someone’s motive is different.
question_source_known: Do you know where or from whom to check the missing fact?
example_source_known: For example: there is a decision-maker or a record of the terms. A second-hand account may be incomplete.
question_explicit_agreement: Did you explicitly agree on the same thing?
example_explicit_agreement: “I will send a draft on Tuesday and you will reply on Wednesday” is clearer than “let’s sort it out later”.
question_inference_distinguished: Can you separate a fact from your interpretation?
example_inference_distinguished: “There is no reply” is a fact. “They don’t respect me” is one possible interpretation while the reason is unknown.
question_contrary_evidence: Is there a fact that does not fit your explanation?
example_contrary_evidence: For example: you expect no help, but the person has already offered another time.
question_falsification_criterion: Do you know what fact would make you change your mind?
example_falsification_criterion: For example: a clear reply or a kept promise would show that your earlier explanation was incomplete.
question_goal_is_own: Is this change something you personally want?
example_goal_is_own: Imagine nobody would praise or criticise you. Would you still want to take this step?
question_undesired_outcome_known: Do you know which outcome would be unacceptable to you?
example_undesired_outcome_known: For example: gaining agreement at the cost of constant overload, or preserving a relationship by abandoning your limit.
question_value_named: Can you name what matters most to you here?
example_value_named: For example: peace of mind, mutual effort, independence, finishing a task or keeping time for family.
question_cost_acceptable: Is the cost of the step acceptable to you right now?
example_cost_acceptable: Consider time, money, fatigue and commitments. A manageable step need not use everything at once.
question_values_share_constraint: Are two important wishes competing for the same resource?
example_values_share_constraint: For example: work and loved ones both need the same free evening. You cannot promise the whole evening to both.
question_goal_wanted_with_resources: If you had enough time and energy, would you still want this?
example_goal_wanted_with_resources: This can separate “it matters, but I’m tired” from “I don’t want it, but feel obliged”.
question_available_time_known: Do you have a specific time for a small step?
example_available_time_known: For example: ten minutes after breakfast. “Sometime in the evening” may get taken up by other commitments.
question_resource_available: Is what you need for the first step already available?
example_resource_available: Check specifically: the file opens, the money is available, materials are at hand or help is confirmed.
question_skill_available: Can you already do a small part of the task?
example_skill_available: For example: complete one item, draft a request or repeat a familiar exercise.
question_info_access: Can you obtain the information in an available way?
example_info_access: For example: open a document or ask someone who has agreed to discuss the topic.
question_previous_attempt_effect: Did the previous attempt change anything at all?
example_previous_attempt_effect: For example: there is still no answer, but you learned whom to ask or which step was too large.
question_small_step_possible: Can you take one small step now?
example_small_step_possible: Even one rough item is a step. If that is unavailable too, choose a pause and a time to return.
question_decision_owner_known: Do you know who can make the needed decision?
example_decision_owner_known: For example: a manager approves it, you decide yourself or two people need to agree.
question_other_agreement: Has the other person agreed to take part?
example_other_agreement: Wanting help is not the same as having agreement. An explicit yes to a specific request counts.
question_external_dependency: Does the next result depend on someone else’s action?
example_external_dependency: For example: you can prepare an application, but another person makes the decision.
question_independent_alternative: Is there a useful step you can take independently?
example_independent_alternative: For example: prepare your own option, check the terms or finish a part that needs no approval.
question_contact_safe: Is it safe and appropriate to discuss this with the person now?
example_contact_safe: If a conversation involves threats, pressure or ignoring an explicit refusal, choose an independent step without contact.
question_waiting_deadline_known: Have you decided how long you are willing to wait?
example_waiting_deadline_known: For example: wait until the agreed date, then choose another option instead of checking messages endlessly.
question_nonnegotiable_constraint: Is there a constraint you cannot change right now?
example_nonnegotiable_constraint: For example: a work schedule, a required payment or someone actually being unavailable.
question_voluntary_commitment: Did you take on this commitment voluntarily?
example_voluntary_commitment: Recall exactly what you promised. Someone else’s expectation may differ from your explicit agreement.
question_reversible_step: Can you try this step and undo it without major cost?
example_reversible_step: A draft can be rewritten and a short trial stopped. A large payment or public promise is harder to undo.
question_stop_condition_known: Do you know when to stop?
example_stop_condition_known: For example: ten minutes are up, tension has risen or the other person has declined to continue.
question_scale_limit_known: Have you set a limit on time, money or effort?
example_scale_limit_known: For example: no more than half an hour, no new spending and no promises on someone else’s behalf.
question_clear_scope: Is it clear what your step includes and what it leaves out for now?
example_clear_scope: For example: write a draft today, then discuss it and make the final decision later.
answerUnknown: This is still unknown. Let’s see what you can check without guessing.
